title: Value vs Reference Types
interviewQuestion: What are value types and reference types in C#, and how does assignment behave differently for each?
summary: Value types copy their data on assignment; reference types copy only the address, so mutations through one alias are visible through all others.

title: Boxing and Unboxing
interviewQuestion: What is boxing and unboxing in C#, and why does it hurt performance?
summary: Boxing/unboxing convert value types to and from heap-allocated objects at a real performance cost, which generics were designed to eliminate.

title: Struct vs Class
interviewQuestion: What is a struct? When should you use a class vs a struct?
summary: Struct is the deliberate choice for small, immutable, content-compared values created in bulk; class remains the default for identity, mutability, and behavior.

title: Record vs Class
interviewQuestion: What is a record? When would you use it instead of a class?
summary: Records give reference types value equality and non-destructive updates, making them ideal for immutable data like DTOs, while classes remain the default for identity and mutable behavior.

title: Why Strings Are Immutable
interviewQuestion: Why are strings immutable in C#, and why is the string class sealed?
summary: Strings are immutable to guarantee thread safety, safe interning, stable hashing, and security, and are sealed to keep those guarantees from being subverted by a subclass.

title: String vs StringBuilder
interviewQuestion: What's the difference between string and StringBuilder, and when would you choose one over the other?
summary: string's immutability makes loop concatenation quadratic and wasteful; StringBuilder's mutable buffer makes it the right tool for loops and large text assembly.

title: C# Data Types and Why They Exist
interviewQuestion: What are the core C# data types like int, char, double, and string, and why do we need types at all?
summary: C#'s type system trades a small amount of upfront thought for memory efficiency, compile-time safety, correct operator semantics, and self-documenting code — and picking decimal over double for money is the most interview-tested example.

title: const vs readonly
interviewQuestion: What's the difference between const and readonly, and why do we need both?
summary: const bakes a compile-time literal into every caller and risks a versioning trap across assemblies; readonly is evaluated at runtime, supports any type, and is the correct tool for values fixed once per instance or app lifetime, including DI dependencies.

title: ref vs out Parameters
interviewQuestion: What's the difference between ref and out parameters in C#?
summary: ref lets a method modify an already-initialized caller variable in place; out lets a method hand back extra results without requiring prior initialization, with TryParse/TryGetValue as the defining real-world pattern.

title: Hash Table, Dictionary and HashSet
interviewQuestion: What is a hash table, and how do Dictionary and HashSet use it?
summary: Hash tables achieve O(1) average lookup by calculating a bucket address from a key's hash rather than searching; Dictionary maps keys to values and HashSet tracks unique keys, with neither guaranteeing enumeration order.

title: Loops in C# and When to Use Each
interviewQuestion: Explain the different loop types in C# and when you'd use each one.
summary: Choose for for indexed/counted work, while for unknown-length condition-gated work, do-while when the body must run at least once, and foreach for safe, index-free iteration of any collection.

title: The using Keyword
interviewQuestion: What does the using keyword do in C#, and why does it matter for resource management?
summary: using guarantees deterministic Dispose() calls even across exceptions, which is essential for unmanaged resources the GC doesn't manage — missing it is the classic cause of connection pool exhaustion.

title: Constructor and Destructor
interviewQuestion: What is a constructor and a destructor in C#, and should you use destructors in modern code?
summary: Constructors initialize objects deterministically at creation; destructors/finalizers run unpredictably on GC collection and should be avoided in favor of IDisposable + using for deterministic resource cleanup.

title: Access Modifiers
interviewQuestion: What are the access modifiers in C#, and what does each one control?
summary: C#'s access modifiers form a spectrum of encapsulation from private (same class) to public (everywhere), with protected internal (OR) and private protected (AND) giving fine-grained control across the assembly and inheritance axes.

title: Serialization and Deserialization
interviewQuestion: What is serialization and deserialization in C#, and where is it used in real applications?
summary: Serialization converts a live object into a transferable format like JSON and deserialization reconstructs it, forming the invisible request/response backbone of every Web API.

title: var vs dynamic
interviewQuestion: What's the difference between var and dynamic in C#?
summary: var infers and locks a variable's type at compile time with full static checking and zero overhead; dynamic defers all type resolution to runtime via the DLR, trading compile-time safety for flexibility at a real performance cost.

title: Compile Time vs Runtime
interviewQuestion: What's the difference between compile time and runtime in C#, and which errors get caught at each stage?
summary: Compile time catches structural/type errors and resolves overloading before anything runs; runtime is when the program executes, throws logic errors, and resolves overriding dynamically.

title: Stack vs Heap and Heap Allocation
interviewQuestion: What is heap allocation? Explain the difference between the stack and the heap.
summary: The stack offers fast, automatic memory for locals and references, while the heap holds every reference-type object's actual data under GC management — heap allocation's extra cost and GC pressure is the root cause behind performance anti-patterns like boxing and loop string concatenation.

title: IL, JIT and CLR
interviewQuestion: What are IL, JIT, and CLR, and how do they fit together in the .NET execution model?
summary: C# compiles to CPU-independent IL, the JIT translates that IL into native machine code per method at runtime, and the CLR is the overarching engine hosting memory management, type safety, security, and exception handling around the whole process.

title: Garbage Collection
interviewQuestion: Explain how garbage collection works in .NET, including generations.
summary: The GC reclaims unreachable heap memory via Mark-Sweep-Compact, uses generations to make short-lived-object collection cheap and frequent while long-lived-object collection stays rare, and — critically — only manages memory, never unmanaged resources, which is why IDisposable and using remain essential and GC.Collect() should never be called manually.

title: The Four Pillars of OOP
interviewQuestion: What are the pillars of OOP?
summary: The four pillars — Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, Polymorphism — work together to protect state, simplify usage, reuse structure, and let one call adapt to many types.

title: What Is an Abstract Class?
interviewQuestion: What is an abstract class?
summary: An abstract class cannot be instantiated but delivers shared implemented code plus a compiler-enforced abstract contract that every concrete subclass must fulfill.

title: Interfaces — Abstract Class vs Interface
interviewQuestion: What is an interface? Abstract class vs Interface?
summary: Interfaces are pure, stateless contracts for unrelated 'can-do' capabilities implemented many at a time; abstract classes carry real shared code for genuinely related 'is-a' hierarchies inherited one at a time.

title: Polymorphism and Its Types
interviewQuestion: Explain Polymorphism and its types
summary: Overloading is compiler-resolved by differing signatures at compile time for caller convenience; overriding is runtime-resolved by the actual object type via virtual/override for system extensibility.

title: Shadowing (Hiding) vs Overriding
interviewQuestion: Shadowing (Hiding) vs Overriding
summary: Overriding dispatches by the object's actual runtime type for consistent polymorphic behavior; shadowing (new) dispatches by the reference's declared type, so the result depends on which reference you're holding.

title: Why and When Do You Use Overriding?
interviewQuestion: Why and when do you use Overriding?
summary: Override to replace one varying step in a shared workflow or to extend base behavior — never to opt a type out of its base contract, which signals a Liskov Substitution Principle violation instead.

title: What Is the base Keyword Used For?
interviewQuestion: What is the base keyword used for?
summary: base calls the parent's constructor (which always runs first), lets you extend rather than replace an overridden method, and reaches a member hidden by `new` — but only ever one level up the hierarchy.

title: Static Class — What and Why
interviewQuestion: What is a static class and why use it?
summary: A static class can never be instantiated and requires every member to be static, making it ideal for stateless utilities — unlike a sealed class, which allows instantiation but blocks further inheritance.

title: What Is a Static Variable/Member?
interviewQuestion: What is a static variable/member?
summary: Static members belong to the type with one shared copy across all instances — powerful for true type-level state, but risky as mutable shared state in concurrent web apps, where a DI-managed singleton is usually the safer choice.

title: SOLID Principles — With Real-World Analogies
interviewQuestion: Explain SOLID — with real-world analogies
summary: SOLID is one coherent discipline — via SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, and DIP — for building software that can be extended, tested, and safely changed for years without demolishing what already works.

title: Tightly Coupled vs Loosely Coupled
interviewQuestion: Tightly coupled vs Loosely coupled
summary: Tight coupling welds a class to one concrete implementation, making swaps and testing hard; loose coupling depends on an injected abstraction, making swaps a one-line DI change and testing trivial — but only for dependencies with real behavior, not simple data objects.

title: What Design Patterns Have You Used?
interviewQuestion: What design patterns have you used?
summary: Design patterns organize into Creational, Structural, and Behavioural families, each solving a recurring shape of problem — and a strong interview answer leads with real, defensible project usage over textbook memorization.

title: The Template Method Pattern
interviewQuestion: What is the Template Method pattern?
summary: Template Method locks an algorithm's step order in a base class method and opens only the genuinely varying step(s) to subclasses via protected abstract/virtual — combining real shared code with a compiler-enforced contract that only an abstract class can provide.

title: Delegate and Event Pattern
interviewQuestion: Delegate and Event pattern
summary: A delegate is a type-safe method pointer; an event restricts that delegate to subscribe/unsubscribe-only access from outside, safely enabling one publisher to notify many independent subscribers without either side knowing about the other's details.

title: implicit and explicit Operator Keywords
interviewQuestion: implicit and explicit operator keywords
summary: implicit conversions run automatically and must always be safe and lossless; explicit conversions require a visible cast because data could be lost or the conversion needs deliberate confirmation — exactly mirroring int-to-long vs double-to-int in the built-in numeric model.

title: What Does the Colon Mean in Class Declarations?
interviewQuestion: What does : mean in public class PdfReport : Report?
summary: The colon in a class declaration means inheritance from exactly one base class (listed first) plus any number of interfaces — the same symbol takes on entirely different meanings for constructor chaining, generic constraints, and the ternary operator elsewhere in C#.

title: Task vs Thread
interviewQuestion: What is the difference between Task and Thread in C#, and when would you use each?
summary: Task is a lightweight, pooled, value-returning abstraction over the thread pool that powers async/await, while raw Thread is a heavy, manually-managed OS thread reserved for niche dedicated-worker scenarios.

title: async/await — What Happens Under the Hood
interviewQuestion: Explain async/await — and what happens under the hood.
summary: async/await frees a thread during I/O waits by compiling the method into a resumable state machine, boosting scalability without making any single operation run faster.

title: CancellationToken — Cooperative Cancellation
interviewQuestion: What is a CancellationToken and when have you used it?
summary: CancellationToken provides cooperative, not forceful, cancellation — running code must actively check and propagate it down every layer of a call chain to actually stop.

title: Parallel Programming in C#
interviewQuestion: Explain parallel programming in C# and how you ensure thread safety.
summary: Parallel programming uses multiple CPU cores to speed up CPU-bound work via Parallel.For/ForEach or PLINQ, but any shared mutable state must be protected with Interlocked, locks, or thread-safe collections.

title: IEnumerable vs ICollection vs IList vs IQueryable vs IAsyncEnumerable
interviewQuestion: Explain the difference between IEnumerable, ICollection, IList, IQueryable, and IAsyncEnumerable.
summary: IEnumerable, ICollection, and IList add increasing in-memory capability; IQueryable defers execution to the database via expression trees; and IAsyncEnumerable streams results one item at a time asynchronously.

title: LINQ — Language Integrated Query
interviewQuestion: What is LINQ? Explain the common LINQ methods and the differences between First, Single, and their OrDefault variants.
summary: LINQ offers one uniform, deferred-execution query language across collections, databases, and XML, with First/Single differing precisely in how they handle zero versus multiple matches.

title: Difference between ASP.NET and ASP.NET Core
interviewQuestion: What is the difference between ASP.NET (Framework) and ASP.NET Core?
summary: ASP.NET Core is a ground-up, cross-platform rewrite of ASP.NET Framework — faster, open source, with built-in DI and an explicit middleware pipeline replacing web.config and Global.asax.

title: What is Middleware? Build a custom one.
interviewQuestion: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core, and how would you write a custom middleware component?
summary: Middleware is an ordered, composable pipeline of request/response handlers where registration order determines what each component can see and short-circuit.

title: What is Dependency Injection and its uses?
interviewQuestion: What is Dependency Injection, what are its uses, and how do you choose between Transient, Scoped, and Singleton?
summary: Dependency Injection decouples classes from their dependencies via constructor injection, and choosing the right lifetime — Transient, Scoped, or Singleton — is what prevents state from leaking across unrelated requests.

title: What is Routing?
interviewQuestion: What is routing in ASP.NET Core and how does it map URLs to controller actions?
summary: Routing matches an incoming URL to the exact controller/action that should handle it — via conventional or attribute routing — and must resolve before authentication/authorization can act on the matched endpoint's metadata.

title: What are Filters? What is an Action Filter?
interviewQuestion: What are filters in ASP.NET Core MVC, and what is an action filter specifically?
summary: Filters are MVC-pipeline checkpoints (Authorization, Resource, Action, Exception, Result) that, unlike middleware, have direct access to action context like ModelState and the action's result.

title: How do you handle Global Exception handling in .NET Core?
interviewQuestion: How do you implement global exception handling in ASP.NET Core?
summary: Global exception handling should wrap the entire pipeline via middleware registered first, logging full detail internally while returning only a safe, correlated response mapped to the correct HTTP status code.

title: What is a Minimal API and when would you use it over controllers?
interviewQuestion: What is a Minimal API in ASP.NET Core, and when would you use it instead of controllers?
summary: Minimal APIs trade the MVC controller ceremony for direct, lightweight endpoint definitions in Program.cs — ideal for small/focused services, while Controllers' full pipeline still wins for large, complex APIs.

title: REST API design and HTTP status codes
interviewQuestion: How do you design a RESTful API, and what HTTP status codes should each operation return?
summary: REST design uses plural-noun resource URLs, the correct HTTP verb per action, and precise status codes — with PUT idempotent and POST not, and 401 vs 403 marking unauthenticated versus unauthorized.

title: Explain the ASP.NET Core MVC life cycle
interviewQuestion: Walk me through the complete ASP.NET Core MVC request life cycle, step by step.
summary: The MVC life cycle is a strict, ordered sequence from Kestrel through middleware, routing, filters (Authorization, Resource, Action, Result), model binding, and action/result execution, with exception filters wrapping the model-binding-to-result-execution span.

title: Explain JWT and where it is stored
interviewQuestion: Explain how JWT authentication works and where the token should be stored on the client.
summary: JWT is a self-contained, signed token (header.payload.signature) enabling stateless authentication — its payload is readable but tamper-evident, and it should be stored client-side via HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookies rather than localStorage.

title: What is CORS?
interviewQuestion: What is CORS, why does it exist, and how do you configure it in ASP.NET Core?
summary: CORS is a browser-enforced, server-opted-in relaxation of the Same-Origin Policy for cross-origin JavaScript calls — it protects browser users, not APIs, since non-browser clients bypass it entirely.

title: ViewData vs ViewBag vs TempData
interviewQuestion: What is the difference between ViewData, ViewBag, and TempData in ASP.NET MVC?
summary: ViewData and ViewBag are two syntaxes over the same request-scoped dictionary, while TempData persists across exactly one redirect via session/cookies and is read-once unless explicitly kept or peeked.

title: What are Session and Cookies?
interviewQuestion: What are Session and Cookies in ASP.NET Core, and how do they differ?
summary: Cookies are small, client-side, client-visible tokens, while session is larger server-side storage located via a session-ID cookie — and scaling session across multiple servers requires sticky sessions or a distributed cache, which is exactly why many modern APIs prefer stateless JWT instead.

title: SOAP vs REST
interviewQuestion: What's the difference between SOAP and REST, and what is WCF?
summary: SOAP is a strict, XML-only, formally-contracted protocol still favored in regulated enterprise integration, while REST is a lighter, flexible architectural style that dominates modern web/mobile APIs — with WCF as .NET's Address/Binding/Contract-based bridge between the two eras.

title: Code First Migrations — Schema From C#
interviewQuestion: What is Code First? Can we create the schema without an existing database?
summary: Code First lets EF Core generate and evolve the database schema entirely from versioned C# code, with migrations applied as safe, reviewed, idempotent deployment steps rather than blind runtime calls.

title: Eager vs Lazy vs Explicit Loading — and the N+1 Problem
interviewQuestion: Eager vs Lazy vs Explicit Loading — and the N+1 problem?
summary: N+1 is caused by fetching related data one round trip per row instead of batching it — eager loading with Include or, better, projection with Select are the fixes, while lazy loading hides the risk until production load exposes it.

title: The Change Tracker and Its Performance Cost
interviewQuestion: Explain the Change Tracker and how it impacts performance.
summary: The Change Tracker's snapshot-and-compare model makes SaveChanges() work correctly, but its memory and CPU cost scales with how much you load and track — so read-only queries should always use AsNoTracking() and true bulk writes should bypass tracking with ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete.

title: Optimizing EF Core Queries for Large Databases
interviewQuestion: How do you optimize EF Core queries for a large database?
summary: Optimizing EF Core at scale means combining AsNoTracking, projection, deliberate loading strategies, keyset pagination, SARGable queries, bulk operations, and real indexing — and knowing when to step outside the ORM entirely with raw SQL or Dapper.

title: Stored Procedure vs Function
interviewQuestion: What is the difference between a Stored Procedure and a Function in SQL Server, and how does a View differ from both?
summary: Stored procedures are full programs with side effects invoked via EXEC; functions are pure single-value/table returns usable inline; views are just saved queries unless indexed.

title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered Indexes
interviewQuestion: What is the difference between a Clustered and a Non-Clustered index, and what does the INCLUDE clause do?
summary: A clustered index IS the physically sorted table (one per table); non-clustered indexes are separate lookup structures (many per table), and INCLUDE turns them into covering indexes that avoid expensive Key Lookups.

title: What is an Execution Plan?
interviewQuestion: What is an execution plan and how do you use it to diagnose a slow query?
summary: The execution plan reveals SQL Server's real strategy — chase down Scans and Key Lookups, watch for stale statistics via estimated-vs-actual row gaps, and let it guide indexing decisions.

title: How Do You Optimize a Stored Procedure?
interviewQuestion: A stored procedure is running slowly in production. Walk me through how you would diagnose and optimize it.
summary: Optimize a slow procedure by measuring first, then fixing the query, indexing, NOCOUNT, parameter sniffing, and batching large DML — in that order.

title: Transactions in a Stored Procedure
interviewQuestion: How would you implement a money-transfer operation as a transaction in a stored procedure, and what is ACID?
summary: Transactions guarantee ACID via BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK with TRY-CATCH, XACT_ABORT, and @@TRANCOUNT checks — and isolation levels trade consistency for concurrency, with NOLOCK being the risky extreme.

title: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL
interviewQuestion: What are DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL in SQL, and what's the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP?
summary: DDL/DML/DCL/TCL categorize SQL statements by structure, data, permissions, and transaction control — and in SQL Server, TRUNCATE, unlike in Oracle, is fully transactional and rollback-able.

title: Constraints in SQL
interviewQuestion: What constraints does SQL Server support, and why enforce rules at the database level instead of only in application code?
summary: Constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT) enforce data integrity at the database engine level, the one place no application, script, or import can bypass.

title: CTE vs Temp Table vs Table Variable
interviewQuestion: What is a CTE, how is it different from a temp table and a table variable, and when would you use recursion?
summary: CTEs are throwaway, query-scoped, non-materialized (but uniquely recursive); temp tables are real, indexable, statistics-backed session-scoped tables; table variables are lighter batch-scoped tables with weak row estimates.

title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE
interviewQuestion: Explain the difference between ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, and NTILE, and how would you find the 5th highest salary?
summary: ROW_NUMBER is always unique, RANK skips after ties, DENSE_RANK doesn't skip (correct for Nth-highest questions), and NTILE buckets rows evenly — all scoped per group via PARTITION BY.

title: HAVING vs WHERE, and OFFSET-FETCH
interviewQuestion: What's the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and how does OFFSET-FETCH pagination work — what's its main weakness?
summary: WHERE filters rows pre-grouping, HAVING filters groups post-grouping; OFFSET/FETCH paginates but slows on deep pages, which keyset (seek) pagination via a cursor avoids.

title: EXISTS vs IN
interviewQuestion: What's the difference between EXISTS and IN in SQL Server, and why is NOT IN dangerous?
summary: IN materializes a value list to compare against; EXISTS is a correlated, early-exit check — and NOT IN is dangerous because a single NULL in its subquery silently returns zero rows, unlike the NULL-safe NOT EXISTS.

title: Explain JOINs
interviewQuestion: Explain the different types of JOINs in SQL Server, and describe the common trap with LEFT JOIN conditions.
summary: JOIN type controls which unmatched rows survive; LEFT/RIGHT/FULL preserve unmatched rows as NULLs, and a right-table filter belongs in ON, not WHERE, or it silently becomes an INNER JOIN.

title: datetime vs datetime2, @@ROWCOUNT
interviewQuestion: What's the difference between datetime and datetime2 in SQL Server, and what does @@ROWCOUNT return?
summary: datetime2 is the wider-range, higher-precision, storage-efficient successor to the legacy rounding datetime type; @@ROWCOUNT always reflects only the immediately preceding statement, commonly used to drive UPSERT logic.

title: Table Partitioning
interviewQuestion: What is table partitioning in SQL Server, and what problems does it solve?
summary: Partitioning physically splits a huge table into chunks by a key column's ranges while it stays queryable as one table, enabling partition elimination, near-instant archiving via partition switch, and per-partition maintenance.

title: Cursors and Loops — And Why to Avoid Them
interviewQuestion: What is a cursor in SQL Server, and why should you generally avoid them? When is a cursor actually the right tool?
summary: Cursors turn one set operation into N slow row-by-row round-trips (50-1000x slower) — prefer set-based rewrites, and reserve cursors/WHILE loops for genuine per-row side effects or deliberate large-DML batching.

title: Foreign Key/Unique Key Syntax and Normalization
interviewQuestion: Explain FOREIGN KEY and UNIQUE constraint syntax, and what are 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF normalization — when would you deliberately denormalize?
summary: FOREIGN KEY/UNIQUE constraints enforce referential integrity and uniqueness; normalization (1NF/2NF/3NF) eliminates redundancy for transactional integrity, while denormalization is a deliberate, measured trade-off for read performance.

title: Azure App Service vs Functions vs AKS
interviewQuestion: Azure App Service vs Azure Functions vs AKS — when do you use which?
summary: Pick compute by traffic shape and ops budget: App Service for steady always-on apps, Functions for event-driven bursty work, and AKS only when you truly need Kubernetes-level orchestration across many services.

title: Service Bus vs Event Grid vs Event Hub
interviewQuestion: Azure Service Bus vs Event Grid vs Event Hub — what's the difference and when do you use each?
summary: Choose Azure messaging by the guarantee you need: Service Bus for durable commands, Event Grid for lightweight reactive notifications, and Event Hub for massive replayable telemetry streams.

title: Managing Secrets: Key Vault and Managed Identity
interviewQuestion: How do you manage secrets in Azure?
summary: Keep secrets out of source control entirely — user-secrets locally, Key Vault in production, accessed via Managed Identity so there's no credential left to leak.

title: Azure API Management — The API Gateway
interviewQuestion: What is Azure API Management and why use it?
summary: APIM is the managed gateway that gives clients one secured entry point while centralizing auth, rate limiting, transformation, and analytics so backends can evolve freely underneath.

title: Git Branching — Merge vs Rebase
interviewQuestion: How do you work with Git — branching strategy, and merge vs rebase?
summary: Merge is the safe default for shared branches because it never rewrites history; rebase is a cleanup tool reserved strictly for your own local, unpushed commits.

title: CI/CD with Azure DevOps
interviewQuestion: How do you implement CI/CD with Azure DevOps?
summary: CI catches problems within minutes of every push; CD turns that validated build into a series of gated, slot-based, reversible promotions all the way to production.

title: Writing Unit Tests — AAA, xUnit, and Moq
interviewQuestion: How do you write unit tests?
summary: Unit tests isolate one class with mocked dependencies via AAA, and dependency injection through interfaces is what makes that isolation — and therefore real unit testing — possible at all.

title: What to Look for in a Code Review
interviewQuestion: What do you look for in a code review?
summary: A good code review follows a strict priority order — correctness and security before performance and style — because catching a structural flaw matters far more than catching a naming nitpick.

title: Security Best Practices in .NET
interviewQuestion: What are the security best practices you follow in .NET?
summary: Application security is layered defense — parameterized queries, salted password hashing, default Razor encoding with HttpOnly cookies, anti-forgery tokens, Key Vault secrets, server-side authorization, and DTO binding each close one specific attack path.

title: Project Architecture — Layered / Clean Architecture
interviewQuestion: Explain your project architecture.
summary: Clean/N-tier architecture keeps business rules centralized and swappable by making every dependency point inward toward a Domain core that depends on nothing.

title: Microservices vs Monolith
interviewQuestion: What are microservices? Would you use them here?
summary: Microservices trade a monolith's simplicity for independent scaling and failure isolation, but only pay off with real service boundaries, async messaging, and Saga-based consistency — not by default.

title: Designing a URL Shortener (High Read-Traffic System)
interviewQuestion: How would you design a URL shortener / a system handling high read traffic?
summary: System design questions reward a structured process — requirements, API, data model, then scaling the dominant traffic pattern (usually reads via caching) — over a single 'correct' architecture.

title: Designing for Scalability
interviewQuestion: How do you design for scalability?
summary: Scalability is achieved by measuring the real bottleneck and attacking it in cost order — cache, database, stateless app tier, async offload, CDN — with sharding reserved as a last, expensive resort.

title: Caching — Levels, Patterns, and Invalidation
interviewQuestion: What is caching? What are the strategies?
summary: Caching is a hierarchy of increasingly fast, increasingly limited stores in front of the database, and the entire discipline reduces to choosing what's safe to serve stale and knowing exactly when it stopped being fresh.

title: Idempotent Payment API — Preventing Duplicate Charges
interviewQuestion: How would you design an idempotent payment API (prevent duplicate payments)?
summary: True idempotency comes from an atomic database unique constraint that claims a client-generated key before charging, not from a check-then-act pattern or a disabled UI button.

title: Handling Concurrency — Two Users Editing the Same Record
interviewQuestion: How do you handle concurrency — two users editing the same record?
summary: Default to optimistic concurrency with a rowversion check, reserve pessimistic locking for frequent expensive conflicts, and replace both with a single atomic conditional UPDATE for simple counters like stock.

title: Monolith vs Layered vs Clean vs CQRS — How Do You Choose?
interviewQuestion: Monolith vs Layered vs Clean vs CQRS — how do you choose?
summary: Each architecture pattern — Layered, Clean, CQRS, Event Sourcing — is justified by a specific concrete requirement, and the senior default is to start simple and add structure only when real pain proves it's needed.

title: Designing Background Jobs / Scheduled Tasks in .NET
interviewQuestion: How do you design a background job / scheduled task in .NET?
summary: A .NET background job must create a fresh DI scope per iteration, never let exceptions kill its loop, honor graceful shutdown, and be designed as idempotent since scaling out will otherwise run it multiple times concurrently.

title: Making an API Resilient to a Failing Dependency
interviewQuestion: How do you make an API resilient to a failing dependency?
summary: API resilience is a layered defense — timeout, backoff retry, circuit breaker, fallback, and bulkhead isolation — where a missing timeout alone is the most common cause of a partial failure becoming a total outage.

title: Monitoring a Production .NET Application
interviewQuestion: How do you monitor a production .NET application?
summary: Production observability requires three complementary pillars — structured logs, percentile-based metrics, and distributed tracing — because no single one can answer both 'what happened' and 'where exactly did the time go'.

title: Configuration Across Environments
interviewQuestion: How do you handle configuration across environments?
summary: Configuration should follow a documented precedence chain, keep secrets in a dedicated secret manager, and validate strongly-typed options at startup so misconfiguration fails immediately rather than silently in production.

title: Walking Through the Full Request Lifecycle
interviewQuestion: Walk me through what happens when a user hits your API endpoint.
summary: Understanding the full request lifecycle — from DNS through the ordered middleware pipeline, DI-scoped services, EF Core, and back — including the easy-to-forget final scope disposal, is what distinguishes real production experience from textbook knowledge.

title: Two Sum
interviewQuestion: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
summary: Two Sum is the canonical lesson in trading memory for speed: a Dictionary lookup turns an O(n²) brute force into O(n).

title: Contains Duplicate / Find Duplicates in an Array
interviewQuestion: Given an array, determine if it contains any duplicate values, and separately, return the list of values that appear more than once.
summary: HashSet.Add's boolean return value is a free, single-pass duplicate detector — no separate Contains check needed.

title: Find Duplicate Characters in a Word (with Counts)
interviewQuestion: Given a word, find every character that repeats and how many times each one occurs.
summary: GetValueOrDefault turns character counting into a one-line accumulate, and a second pass over the map reports the duplicates.

title: First Non-Repeated Character
interviewQuestion: Find the first character in a string that does not repeat.
summary: Finding the first unique character needs two passes: count everything first, then re-walk the ORIGINAL order to find the first count-of-1.

title: Reverse a String (with a Loop)
interviewQuestion: Reverse a string without using a built-in Reverse method, and also handle reversing the words in a sentence.
summary: String immutability forces a char-array copy, but the two-pointer swap-and-converge pattern reverses it in O(n) time.

title: Palindrome — String and Number
interviewQuestion: Determine whether a string is a palindrome, and separately, whether an integer is a palindrome without converting it to a string.
summary: String palindromes use converging two pointers; numeric palindromes reverse only half the digits arithmetically to dodge overflow.

title: Prime Number Check
interviewQuestion: Write a function to check whether a given number is prime, and explain why you only loop up to its square root.
summary: Prime checking only needs to test divisors up to √n, since factor pairs always mirror around the square root — O(√n) instead of O(n).

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
interviewQuestion: Given an array of stock prices by day, find the maximum profit from a single buy and a single sell (buy must occur before sell).
summary: A single pass tracking the running minimum price turns an O(n²) pair search into an O(n) greedy scan.

title: Plus One (Big Number as Digit Array)
interviewQuestion: Given a non-negative integer represented as an array of its digits, add one to it and return the new array of digits.
summary: Plus One simulates manual carry propagation from the rightmost digit, growing the array by one only in the all-9s edge case.

title: Roman to Integer
interviewQuestion: Convert a Roman numeral string (e.g., "MCMXCIV") to its integer value.
summary: A single lookahead comparison — current value less than next means subtract — decodes Roman numeral subtractive notation in one linear pass.

title: Linked List — The Five Classics
interviewQuestion: Solve the five most-asked linked list problems: reverse a list, detect a cycle, find the middle node, merge two sorted lists, and remove the Nth node from the end.
summary: Most linked-list interview problems reduce to holding 2-3 pointers and moving them at carefully chosen relative speeds or offsets.

title: Array Classics
interviewQuestion: Solve five classic in-place array problems: move zeroes to the end, find the maximum subarray sum, rotate an array by k, find the second largest element, and merge two sorted arrays in place.
summary: Array classics reduce to a handful of patterns: insert-pointer compaction, extend-or-restart running sums, reversal-based rotation, and directionally-correct in-place merging.

title: Dictionary/HashSet Classics
interviewQuestion: Solve five classic hashmap/hashset problems: valid anagram, group anagrams, word frequency count, majority element, and array intersection.
summary: Dictionary and HashSet reduce anagram checks, grouping, frequency counting, majority finding, and intersection problems to a single linear pass each.

title: Infinite Loops and FizzBuzz
interviewQuestion: Show the different ways to write an infinite loop in C#, identify a common accidental infinite loop bug, and implement FizzBuzz.
summary: Infinite loops are fine when intentional and exitable, dangerous when accidental (missing an increment); FizzBuzz's trick is checking the most specific condition first.

title: Complexity Revision Table
interviewQuestion: Summarize the time and space complexity of the classic coding problems, and describe your live-coding protocol for tackling a new problem in an interview.
summary: Nearly every classic coding problem is a two-pointer trick or a hash lookup, and a disciplined six-step live-coding protocol turns any new problem into a structured, demonstrable process.

title: Investigating a Slow SQL Query
interviewQuestion: How would you investigate a slow query?
summary: Diagnose slow queries with hard evidence — logical reads, the actual execution plan, and SARGability — not intuition about the SQL text.

title: Why Did the API Suddenly Become Slow?
interviewQuestion: If an API suddenly became slow, where do you start?
summary: Sudden API slowness is diagnosed by scoping impact, identifying what changed, following the trace to the slowest hop, and mitigating before root-causing.

title: Debugging a Memory Leak / High Memory Usage
interviewQuestion: How do you debug a memory leak / high memory usage?
summary: Debug memory leaks by confirming true unbounded growth, comparing dump snapshots to find the growing type, and matching it to known .NET causes like captive dependencies, unsubscribed events, or unbounded caches.

title: A User Reports Data Is Wrong — How to Investigate
interviewQuestion: A user reports data is wrong. How do you investigate?
summary: Investigate wrong data by reproducing the exact case and repeatedly splitting the search space — API vs. client, write vs. read — before checking cache, timezone, precision, and join pitfalls.

title: How to Handle a Production Incident
interviewQuestion: How do you handle a production incident?
summary: Handle production incidents by mitigating impact first through rollback, scaling, flags, or failover, communicating throughout, and only root-causing via a blameless post-mortem once service is restored.

title: Agile/Scrum Ceremonies and Your Role
interviewQuestion: Explain Agile/Scrum and your role in it.
summary: Scrum is a fixed rhythm of five ceremonies and three roles that turns big, risky releases into small, demoable, honestly-tracked increments.

title: Answering Behavioral Questions with STAR
interviewQuestion: Tell me about a time you faced a tough situation at work. (Behavioral — use STAR)
summary: STAR turns a vague behavioral answer into evidence: brief context, your specific responsibility, your concrete actions, and a measurable result every single time.

title: Smart Questions to Ask the Interviewer
interviewQuestion: Do you have any questions for us?
summary: The best closing interview questions target real day-to-day signal — tech stack, type of work, onboarding, and release cadence — turning the moment into a genuine evaluation, not small talk.

title: Integrating Azure OpenAI into a .NET Core App
interviewQuestion: How do you integrate Azure OpenAI with a .NET Core application?
summary: Integrating Azure OpenAI into .NET is less about the API call itself and more about Singleton lifecycle, Managed Identity auth, resilience (Polly), streaming, and cost/security discipline around it.

title: Semantic Kernel — Orchestrating LLMs in .NET
interviewQuestion: What is Semantic Kernel?
summary: Semantic Kernel is the orchestration layer around raw LLM calls in .NET, turning your existing C# services into model-callable tools via Plugins, chaining multi-step work via Planners, and grounding answers via Memory/RAG.

title: RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) in .NET
interviewQuestion: Explain RAG — can you implement it in .NET?
summary: RAG grounds LLM answers in your real, permission-aware documents by retrieving the most relevant chunks via (ideally hybrid) vector search and injecting them into the prompt, with citations for verifiability.

title: Prompt vs Completion, and Handling Token Limits
interviewQuestion: Prompt vs Completion, and how do you handle token limits?
summary: Prompt and completion are both billed and share one context-window budget, so disciplined token counting, context truncation, rolling-summary chat history, and explicit MaxTokens reservation are what keep LLM calls reliable and affordable.

title: Building a .NET API That Talks to an LLM
interviewQuestion: How would you build a .NET API that interacts with an LLM?
summary: A production LLM-backed .NET API is mostly ordinary API engineering — auth, rate limiting, caching, async/streaming, Polly resilience, and prompt-injection-aware guardrails — wrapped around a comparatively small LLM call.
